# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The Museum of Unfinished Things occupied a narrow brick building between a locksmith and a bakery that made excellent but structurally questionable cakes. It was easy to miss. There was no gold lettering above the door, no statue of a famous person holding an unfinished masterpiece, no queue of tourists taking pictures with their lips pursed in thought.

The sign simply read:

**MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS**  
**Please do not finish anything while inside.**

I had worked there for seven months as the night attendant. My duties were modest: lock the front door at six, walk through three galleries, ensure that no visitor became overexcited and attempted to complete an exhibit, and turn off the lamps in the reading room.

I was good at my job, especially the final part.

At closing time, the last visitors gathered their coats and children and stepped into the rain. Then the doors shut, the city withdrew, and the museum became a place where the abandoned efforts of strangers sat quietly under glass.

There was a staircase with no final step.

A letter whose last page was blank.

A clock stopped at ten minutes past six.

A city map showing a bridge that stopped halfway across the river.

A violin missing its highest string.

A loaf of bread rising beneath an overturned bucket.

There was also a jar of screws, all of them slightly different sizes, labelled **MISCELLANEOUS. WE THOUGHT THEY MIGHT NEED SOMETHING.**

I loved it.

Not because everything in the museum was beautiful, though some things were. I loved it because nothing there made a persuasive argument about what it was supposed to become. A staircase was allowed to be incomplete without being called a failure. The bread could remain under its bucket indefinitely, slowly becoming less bread-like, without anyone rushing in to save it.

That was a luxury I had not appreciated until I started working there.

On my first night, I straightened a wooden cradle whose left leg was half an inch shorter than the other three. The next morning, a note appeared beneath it.

**Please leave the tilt alone. It is the most honest thing in the room.**

The note was unsigned. The next night, when I walked past the cradle, I heard someone laugh behind the wall.

After that, I tried not to touch the exhibits.

## The Staircase Without a Final Step

At twelve minutes past midnight, the staircase spoke.

I wish I could say it made a sound. It did not creak, cough, or politely request my attention. It simply occurred to me that I could hear footsteps climbing it.

I went into the central gallery carrying my little flashlight, though I had never needed it before. The power was always on, and the museum had the pale, sleepless brightness of a place where nothing was allowed to decay.

The staircase rose from the far wall in fourteen brass steps. I had inspected it hundreds of times. It was a beautiful object: polished wood, a thin black handrail, a small placard explaining that the unknown architect had abandoned the commission after the fourteenth step.

Above the final step was a blank wall.

Now there was a door.

It was painted the same off-white as the wall, outlined in a thin line of tarnished silver. A brass plate hung at eye level.

**FOR THE UNFINISHED VISITOR**

I considered the wording.

I considered the hour.

I considered the fact that I had spent the afternoon failing to finish an email to my landlord.

Then I opened the door.

Beyond it was a corridor much larger than the museum. Its walls were hung with framed moments: a man standing on a railway platform, a woman reaching for a cup on a high shelf, a swimmer balanced at the edge of a diving board. Each frame contained a person caught at the instant before something happened.

The floor was covered in blue carpet. A faint white light shone from nowhere in particular.

At the end of the corridor stood a tall woman in a green coat, holding an umbrella that had not yet been opened.

She looked at me.

“You are late,” she said.

“For what?”

“For the part of your life you keep postponing.”

“I was at work.”

“You are still at work.”

I glanced back down the corridor. The museum had disappeared.

The woman opened her umbrella. It was transparent, and through it I could see a sky crowded with unmade buildings.

“Come,” she said. “There is something you left here.”

## The Letter in Nine Hands

I was not conscious of walking, but when I looked again, I was sitting at a desk in a small room filled with paper.

The letter began:

**Dear Mara,**

The first version ended there.

Another continued:

**Dearest Mara, I know you must think I am a coward. You are probably right. I have thought about writing this letter every day since the funeral, which is an admission that I think too much and act too little, although perhaps it is only an admission that I enjoy punishing myself.**

A third was blunter:

**MARA, I AM SORRY. I AM NOT SORRY. I AM NOT SURE WHICH.**

There were nine versions in all, each written in a different hand, each more exhausted than the last. The final page of each letter was blank.

“I do not understand,” I said. “Why keep all of them?”

The woman in the green coat sat opposite me. In the corridor, she had seemed tall and imperious. Here, she looked tired. There was flour on one sleeve of her coat.

“Because none of them says the true thing.”

“Which is?”

“That I was afraid.”

She pushed the letters toward me.

“And I thought a perfect sentence could make fear disappear. As if language were a kind of medicine. As if, once I found exactly the right words, I would no longer have to act.”

The blank pages seemed to lean away from me.

“What was the true thing?” I asked.

“That I wanted her to forgive me before I had done anything I deserved forgiveness for.”

Outside the room, something knocked.

It was the staircase, climbing its fourteen brass steps, over and over, growing slower each time. Each footstep sounded like a question that had traveled a long distance and forgotten what it meant.

The woman rose.

“Every unfinished thing has a reason,” she said. “Not always a good reason. Sometimes the only reason is that the person was frightened, distracted, unwell, young, or unable to make the world obey the shape of their desire. But there is always a reason.”

The ninth letter lifted from the desk and folded itself into a white bird.

It flew through the window.

## The Machine for Hearing Blue

The blue room was full of machinery.

There were copper tubes, glass chambers, black buttons, coils of silver wire, and a large brass horn pointed toward the ceiling. The machine was labelled **APPARATUS FOR HEARING THE FREQUENCY OF SADNESS**, but someone had crossed out “sadness” and replaced it with “blue.”

That was better. “Blue” was something I understood. Blue could be a colour, a mood, a song, a distance, a bruise, a tie.

The machine played a note when I entered.

Then another.

A third note joined it, forming a chord that seemed to contain an entire weather system. I thought of rain on a roof, a bus pulling away, the blue hour after sunset when the world briefly becomes honest.

A voice came from the machine.

It did not speak words. It produced small sounds: pauses, breaths, a chair scraping, a cup set down, a person trying to say something and deciding not to.

I knew that voice.

Not exactly. It was a voice I had spent twenty-eight years trying to remember without admitting that I wanted to forget it.

I had been eleven when my father left the house at ten past two in the afternoon. He said he was going to buy milk. He wore a brown coat. The milk shop was closed. That was all I knew.

I had begun writing a novel about it.

I had written eleven versions of the first page.

The machine clicked.

A young boy appeared in the glass chamber. He had a scraped knee, a red sweater, and the solemn expression of someone who had been told that adults knew everything.

He looked at me.

“Did you finish it?” he asked.

“What?”

“The story.”

I felt the heat rise in my face. In the museum, my notebook was hidden beneath the desk in the staff room. No one was supposed to know about it. No one was supposed to know that I had spent seven months constructing a father who might have been a monster, a victim, a frightened man, or simply a man who had gone for milk and never returned.

I wanted to say that the story was not about him. I wanted to say that I had abandoned the novel. I wanted to say that the blank pages were evidence of good judgment, not cowardice.

Instead, I said, “No.”

The boy nodded as if this were entirely expected.

“What happens next?”

“I don’t know.”

The machine played a single note.

It sounded like a door opening in a house where no one had spoken for years.

## The Man Building a House

I followed the sound into a gallery I had never entered.

The door was marked **ROOM FOR THE ROAD NOT TAKEN**, but inside there was a half-built house.

Floorboards stretched across the floor. Stud walls rose to the ceiling. A ladder leaned against a beam. On a workbench lay a saw, a hammer, a tape measure, and a loaf of bread with a knife stuck directly into its centre.

A man in paint-stained overalls knelt beside an open paint can. He was perhaps sixty. His white hair had been brushed back from his forehead. He looked up when I entered.

“Careful,” he said. “The floor’s wet.”

The floor was dry.

He noticed me noticing this and smiled.

“Probably,” he said.

The walls were covered in measurements. Some were crossed out. Others had been written over so many times that the paper had torn. Near the window, someone had drawn a chair and then erased it, leaving only the four nail holes.

“Why is it unfinished?” I asked.

The man looked around as if the answer might be hidden somewhere in the house.

“I ran out of certainty,” he said.

“About the house?”

“About the person I thought I would be when I finished it.”

He stood, using the workbench for support.

“I wanted a room exactly like this. I wanted to know that when I put down the last nail, I would finally arrive. That the life I had been rehearsing would become real.”

He picked up the hammer and examined it.

“So I stopped.”

His voice was neither bitter nor proud. It was the voice of someone explaining a habit they expected to be questioned.

“The house is still possible,” he said. “That may be too much to ask.”

Outside, rain had begun to tap against the museum windows. Yet when I looked back, I saw a real roof above the unfinished walls, black tiles shining under a moon that should have been behind the clouds.

The man offered me the hammer.

“Would you like to drive the first nail?”

I took it.

The handle was warm.

I raised it, then lowered it.

“I can’t,” I said.

He nodded.

“Good,” he said. “A nail hammered in too early is only a hole with ambitions.”

## The Sixth Star

The next room was dark except for a ceiling covered in small lights.

They were stars, though not quite the stars I knew. They moved when I was not looking at them. Some formed familiar shapes; others suggested patterns without ever resolving into anything.

A card on the wall read:

**THE CONSTELLATION OF BEGINNINGS**

**The sixth star has not been invented yet.**

A young woman sat beneath the display. She was perhaps twenty, wearing a mustard-colored coat and holding a paper cup gone soft with use. She looked as though she had been waiting for a train that would never arrive.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“You’re the night guard?”

“Among other things.”

She glanced at the ceiling. “What happens if they never find the sixth star?”

“Does it have to be found?”

“That’s what the label says.”

I looked again at the words. The question sounded more complicated than it should have.

I thought of all the futures I had failed to begin: the languages I had abandoned, the friendships I had delayed, the versions of myself that existed only in the margins of other people’s plans.

“What are you beginning?” I asked.

She looked down at her cup.

“I don’t know. I thought I would have figured that out by now.”

“Maybe you’re not old enough.”

“I thought I would be more certain.”

“Most people are not more certain. They are simply better at pretending certainty has no cracks.”

She looked at the stars, and a small smile appeared.

“Would you come back tomorrow?”

“I work nights.”

“Then I suppose I will too.”

The sixth star blinked once above us.

It was not a new star. It was not an answer.

It was simply a light in a place where nobody had decided what it meant.

## What the Founder Wanted

The woman in the green coat was waiting for me in a room with a long table.

Behind her, shelves held thousands of objects. A child’s shoe with one lace missing. A stack of poems. A jar of house keys. A machine for braiding hair that had tangled three strands into a knot no one could undo. Unsent letters, unwritten apologies, dismantled engines, half-built boats, abandoned gardens, and a box of theatre costumes labelled **THE PRODUCTION MAY STILL HAPPEN**.

The woman sat down.

“I am Imogen Vale,” she said. “I founded this museum.”

I looked at her.

“The sign said the museum was founded by a ceramicist.”

“I am a ceramicist. I am also a woman who once believed that potential was a kind of property.”

She turned a cup in her hands.

“When I was young, I made things that collapsed. Bowls cracked. Sculptures leaned. Walls came down. People said I had no patience. They said I was too ambitious. They were not entirely wrong.”

She smiled.

“Then an artist left her final work in my studio. It was a bird made of blue clay. One wing was complete. The other had only the beginning of a wing. The artist had died before she could finish it.”

Imogen looked toward the shelves.

“I wanted to save it. I thought if I could gather all the things people had left behind—the poems, the models, the plans, the almost-finished lives—then nothing would truly be lost. I thought I could build a room where failure did not have to become a verdict.”

Her hand trembled around the cup.

“For a while, it worked. People came here with their abandoned projects. They told me what they had meant to do. Some of them came back years later. A few had finished the things. Most had not.”

“What happened?”

“I realized I had misunderstood the museum.”

She looked at me.

“Potential is not a thing that can be kept. It belongs to the future. If I preserved every beginning, I was not protecting possibility. I was locking it away.”

The room seemed suddenly warmer.

“What should the museum be for, then?” I asked.

Imogen looked toward the dark corridor.

“For reminding people that a beginning is not a sentence. For giving them a place to admit that they do not know. Perhaps for keeping one lamp on until they do.”

At three in the morning, the windows showed a different city.

Not another city entirely. Our city, but altered. The streets were wet with reflected neon. Unbuilt towers rose among familiar rooftops. Signs hung over intersections without words. At the edge of the river, a bridge extended halfway across the water and then became a ribbon of pale mist.

The museum’s exhibits stirred.

The bread lifted its bucket.

The letter unfolded itself.

The clock at ten minutes past six began ticking, but its hands moved backwards.

“Why are they leaving?” I asked.

Imogen stood beside me.

“They are not leaving,” she said. “They are returning.”

“Returning to what?”

“To the place where they can still become something else.”

The front doors opened.

Beyond them waited the city, breathing rain and possibility.

I went back to the reading room for my notebook.

The museum’s silence had changed. It was no longer the silence of objects waiting to be completed. It was the silence of an audience.

I opened the notebook to the first page.

**My father left when I was eleven.**

That was how every version began. I had written the sentence a hundred times, changing the font, the weather, the hour, the coat, the reason for the milk. I had made him cruel, then tired, then misunderstood. I had made myself brave, then bitter, then suspiciously composed.

I could not make myself believable.

I picked up a pen.

“My father left when I was eleven,” I wrote.

The words looked smaller than I had expected.

“He said he was going to buy milk. The shop was closed. I do not know what happened after that.”

I stopped.

A voice came from behind me.

“Does that hurt?”

I turned.

The boy from the machine stood in the doorway. His red sweater was speckled with rain, though no rain had touched the room.

“Yes,” I said.

“Which part?”

“All of it.”

He came closer.

“Do you want him to come back?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to forgive him?”

“I don’t know.”

“Those can be different.”

He sat on the edge of the table.

“Keep writing,” he said.

I wrote:

**I wanted the story to explain what happened. I wanted to know whether I had been abandoned or whether my father had been more afraid than I was. I wanted a reason that did not make either of us too small.**

The pen slipped from my hand.

I did not chase it.

For the first time in seven months, I did not try to hide how lost I was.

## The Door Without a Handle

The white door in the corridor was open.

Beyond it, the city waited beneath a sky beginning to pale at the edges.

Imogen stood nearby.

“Take something with you,” she said.

“I don’t think these things belong to me.”

“They do not. That has never been the point.”

I looked at the exhibits moving through the streets. The letter had become a paper bird. The bridge was still unfinished, but a person had placed a chair at its edge and sat there, watching the water.

“What happens now?” I asked.

“The museum will be emptier.”

“That sounds sad.”

“It may be. Emptiness is often sad when you have filled it with the wrong expectations.”

I looked at my notebook.

“I don’t know how my story ends.”

“Then do not tell me.”

“What if I write something terrible?”

“Then you will have a first draft.”

“What if I never write it again?”

“Then you will have a notebook.”

I laughed. It was not a beautiful laugh. It surprised me.

Imogen smiled.

“Go,” she said.

I stepped through the door.

## An Inventory of Emptiness

At dawn, the museum was quiet.

The staircase was gone. So was the loom, the machine, the bridge model, the letter, the bread, and the boy in the red sweater.

In their places were small brass plaques.

**STAIRCASE, 1892–UNKNOWN**  
**Currently climbing the east side of the building.**

**APPARATUS FOR HEARING BLUE**  
**Last seen near the school.**

**THE CONSTELLATION OF BEGINNINGS**  
**The sixth star remains unnamed.**

On my desk was a note from Imogen.

**The bowl in the central gallery is repaired. The gold is visible. I trust you noticed.**

I hurried to see it.

The chipped bowl I had straightened every night for seven months was no longer chipped. A fine line of gold ran around the fracture, shining gently beneath the glass.

I felt a flush of shame. I had altered an exhibit. I had violated the only rule the museum had.

Then I saw the note again.

**I trust you noticed.**

I sat down.

For the first time since I began working there, I understood that the museum was not asking me to preserve things from change. It was asking me to help them remain capable of change.

A little later, the bakery sent over a croissant.

It was structurally questionable.

I ate it anyway.

## The Blank White Card

The next day, the day curator arrived at nine with a box of new labels.

She was organized, skeptical, and constitutionally suspicious of anything that could not be assigned a date.

“We need clearer descriptions,” she said. “The old labels are too subjective.”

I looked at the brass plaques.

“Maybe that is why they survive.”

She placed a stack of blank white cards on the desk.

“Write something useful.”

I picked up a pen.

For the staircase, I wrote:

**A staircase. It rises farther than it intends to.**

For the bread:

**Bread, yeast, and a bucket. A person may return to this project, or may not.**

For the letter:

**A letter written to someone who has not yet read it. Its ending remains private.**

The curator read over my shoulder.

“These are not explanations,” she said.

“No.”

“They are invitations.”

“Those may be explanations too.”

At closing time, a child stopped in front of the repaired bowl.

“Did you break it?” he asked.

“No.”

“Did you fix it?”

I considered the gold line around the crack.

“Yes,” I said. “But it was already worth keeping.”

Outside, the sky darkened. Somewhere in the city, the brass machine played a note. A window lit. A bridge continued by one more metre.

In the staff room, I opened my notebook to the page where I had finally admitted that I did not know what happened next.

For a long time, I only listened to the rain.

Then I wrote:

**My father left the house at ten past two. The milk shop was closed. That is all I know for certain.**

I read the sentence.

It was unfinished.

I wrote another.

The next room was dark except for a ceiling covered in small lights.

They were stars, though not quite the stars I knew. They moved when I was not looking at them. Some formed familiar shapes; others suggested patterns without ever resolving into anything.

A card on the wall read:

**THE CONSTELLATION OF BEGINNINGS**

**The sixth star has not been invented yet.**

A young woman sat beneath the display. She was perhaps twenty, wearing a mustard-colored coat and holding a paper cup gone soft with use. She looked as though she had been waiting for a train that would never arrive.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“You’re the night guard?”

“Among other things.”

She glanced at the ceiling. “What happens if they never find the sixth star?”

“Does it have to be found?”

“That’s what the label says.”

I looked again at the words. The question sounded more complicated than it should have.

I thought of all the futures I had failed to begin: the languages I had abandoned, the friendships I had delayed, the versions of myself that existed only in the margins of other people’s plans.

“What are you beginning?” I asked.

She looked down at her cup.

“I don’t know. I thought I would have figured that out by now.”

“Maybe you’re not old enough.”

“I thought I would be more certain.”

“Most people are not more certain. They are simply better at pretending certainty has no cracks.”

She looked at the stars, and a small smile appeared.

“Would you come back tomorrow?”

“I work nights.”

“Then I suppose I will too.”

The sixth star blinked once above us.

It was not a new star. It was not an answer.

It was simply a light in a place where nobody had decided what it meant.

The woman in the green coat was waiting for me in a room with a long table.

She smiled.

Her hand trembled around the cup.

“What happened?”

“I realized I had misunderstood the museum.”

She looked at me.

“Potential is not a thing that can be kept. It belongs to the future. If I preserved every beginning, I was not protecting possibility. I was locking it away.”

The room seemed suddenly warmer.

“What should the museum be for, then?” I asked.

Imogen looked toward the dark corridor.

“For reminding people that a beginning is not a sentence. For giving them a place to admit that they do not know. Perhaps for keeping one lamp on until they do.”

## A City Made of Beginnings

At three in the morning, the windows showed a different city.

Not another city entirely. Our city, but altered. The streets were wet with reflected neon. Unbuilt towers rose among familiar rooftops. Signs hung over intersections without words. At the edge of the river, a bridge extended halfway across the water and then became a ribbon of pale mist.

Every window displayed a light that had not been lit.

I saw a staircase climbing the side of a distant apartment building. I saw a loom moving across a square, making cloth for a garment whose shape had not yet been chosen. I saw a brass machine on three legs, playing a chord whenever it passed a person who looked lost.

The museum’s exhibits stirred.

The bread lifted its bucket.

The letter unfolded itself.

The violin produced one clear note after another, climbing toward the missing string and stopping just short of it.

The clock at ten minutes past six began ticking, but its hands moved backwards.

“Why are they leaving?” I asked.

Imogen stood beside me.

“They are not leaving,” she said. “They are returning.”

“Returning to what?”

“To the place where they can still become something else.”

The front doors opened.

Beyond them waited the city, breathing rain and possibility.

## The Story I Had Not Written

I went back to the reading room for my notebook.

The museum’s silence had changed. It was no longer the silence of objects waiting to be completed. It was the silence of an audience.

I opened the notebook to the first page.

**My father left when I was eleven.**

That was how every version began. I had written the sentence a hundred times, changing the font, the weather, the hour, the coat, the reason for the milk. I had made him cruel, then tired, then misunderstood. I had made myself brave, then bitter, then suspiciously composed.

I could not make myself believable.

I picked up a pen.

“My father left when I was eleven,” I wrote.

The words looked smaller than I had expected.

“He said he was going to buy milk. The shop was closed. I do not know what happened after that.”

I stopped.

A voice came from behind me.

“Does that hurt?”

I turned.

The boy from the machine stood in the doorway. His red sweater was speckled with rain, though no rain had touched the room.

“Yes,” I said.

“Which part?”

“All of it.”

He came closer.

“Do you want him to come back?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to forgive him?”

“I don’t know.”

“Those can be different.”

He sat on the edge of the table.

“Keep writing,” he said.

I wrote:

**I wanted the story to explain what happened. I wanted to know whether I had been abandoned or whether my father had been more afraid than I was. I wanted a reason that did not make either of us too small.**

The pen slipped from my hand.

I did not chase it.

For the first time in seven months, I did not try to hide how lost I was.

## The Door Without a Handle

The white door in the corridor was open.

Beyond it, the city waited beneath a sky beginning to pale at the edges.

Imogen stood nearby.

“Take something with you,” she said.

“I don’t think these things belong to me.”

“They do not. That has never been the point.”

I looked at the exhibits moving through the streets. The letter had become a paper bird. The bridge was still unfinished, but a person had placed a chair at its edge and sat there, watching the water.

“What happens now?” I asked.

“The museum will be emptier.”

“That sounds sad.”

“It may be. Emptiness is often sad when you have filled it with the wrong expectations.”

I looked at my notebook.

“I don’t know how my story ends.”

“Then do not tell me.”

“What if I write something terrible?”

“Then you will have a first draft.”

“What if I never write it again?”

“Then you will have a notebook.”

I laughed. It was not a beautiful laugh. It surprised me.

Imogen smiled.

“Go,” she said.

I stepped through the door.

## An Inventory of Emptiness

At dawn, the museum was quiet.

The staircase was gone. So was the loom, the machine, the bridge model, the letter, the bread, and the boy in the red sweater.

In their places were small brass plaques.

**STAIRCASE, 1892–UNKNOWN**  
**Currently climbing the east side of the building.**

**APPARATUS FOR HEARING BLUE**  
**Last seen near the school.**

**THE CONSTELLATION OF BEGINNINGS**  
**The sixth star remains unnamed.**

On my desk was a note from Imogen.

**The bowl in the central gallery is repaired. The gold is visible. I trust you noticed.**

I hurried to see it.

The chipped bowl I had straightened every night for seven months was no longer chipped. A fine line of gold ran around the fracture, shining gently beneath the glass.

I felt a flush of shame. I had altered an exhibit. I had violated the only rule the museum had.

Then I saw the note again.

**I trust you noticed.**

I sat down.

For the first time since I began working there, I understood that the museum was not asking me to preserve things from change. It was asking me to help them remain capable of change.

A little later, the bakery sent over a croissant.

It was structurally questionable.

I ate it anyway.

## The Blank White Card

The next day, the day curator arrived at nine with a box of new labels.

She was organized, skeptical, and constitutionally suspicious of anything that could not be assigned a date.

“We need clearer descriptions,” she said. “The old labels are too subjective.”

I looked at the brass plaques.

“Maybe that is why they survive.”

She placed a stack of blank white cards on the desk.

“Write something useful.”

I picked up a pen.

For the staircase, I wrote:

**A staircase. It rises farther than it intends to.**

For the bread:

**Bread, yeast, and a bucket. A person may return to this project, or may not.**

For the letter:

**A letter written to someone who has not yet read it. Its ending remains private.**

The curator read over my shoulder.

“These are not explanations,” she said.

“No.”

“They are invitations.”

“Those may be explanations too.”

At closing time, a child stopped in front of the repaired bowl.

“Did you break it?” he asked.

“No.”

“Did you fix it?”

I considered the gold line around the crack.

“Yes,” I said. “But it was already worth keeping.”

Outside, the sky darkened. Somewhere in the city, the brass machine played a note. A window lit. A bridge continued by one more metre.

In the staff room, I opened my notebook to the page where I had finally admitted that I did not know what happened next.

For a long time, I only listened to the rain.

Then I wrote:

**My father left the house at ten past two. The milk shop was closed. That is all I know for certain.**

I read the sentence.

It was unfinished.

I wrote another.
